catalog_quote: 3.3. Tone High, mid, low, falling and rising tones were noted. Table 20 presents some roots with fairly consistent tone. High and low tones are switched in Doso, except that H does not become L after a voiced ... obstruent. There is also some evidence of a mid tone level. Many roots, however, are more inconsistent in their tone across varieties. For now, we decline to reconstruct tone for items where tone is too inconsistent to be matched to the series below. We speculate that inconsistent tone may be the result of underlying tone sequences on monovocalic roots, as well as roots that have been reclassified for tone in some of the varieties. (pp. 43-44) ... Table 20. Tones [Mak column]: *L — L: ‘answer’ ɡə̀b, ‘bark’ kwə̀ŋ; *H (nouns) — H: ‘eye’ núŋ, ‘front’ sí, ‘millstone’ ɲí, ‘liver’ ɲí; *H (verbs) — H: ‘eat’ tə́ŋ, ‘push’ tɔ́k, ‘hit’ ɡ͡bə́b, ‘ask’ ɓíp; *M — M: ‘swallow’ mī, ‘thing’ nūŋ.…

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record for Mak; this is the only primary phonological statement about Mak that could be opened. It establishes tone, not stress. Included so the site has a sourced quote for the language; it is not one of the two READALL works.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mak (Lee Mak of Panya and Zoo) is treated as a tone language with H, M, L, falling and rising tones on the wordlist forms; the paper says nothing about stress or accent (neither word occurs in the 83 pages).
new_statements.identity_note: Mak [pbl] = LeeMak, spoken in Panya (Panyam) and Zoo (Zo), Karim Lamido LGA, Taraba State; Blench 2012 and Kleinewillinghöfer 2017 treat Panya and Zo as its two dialects and separate Mak from Maghdi (Tala). Norton & Othaniel 2020 cover both Lee Mak of Panya and Lee Mak of Zoo. Boyd 1989 (unopened) is an Adamawa-Ubangi family survey, not a Mak description.
